did_you_know.text: The psalm’s title identifies it as “A Psalm of David,” indicating from the outset both its poetic nature and its attribution to David.
The psalmist declares, “My heart is steadfast”—his heart is ready and firmly resolved to sing, make music, and honor the LORD.
The psalmist calls on the harp and lyre to awaken, and says that he will awaken the dawn with his singing; this creates a picture of music at daybreak.
The praise is not limited to Israel: the psalmist asks to give thanks to the LORD among the peoples and sing praises to him among the nations.
The LORD’s faithful love is described as higher than the heavens, and his faithfulness as reaching to the skies—an image emphasizing their immense extent.
After offering praise, the psalmist asks that God be exalted above the heavens and that his glory be over all the earth, meaning that God’s presence and glory would be seen throughout the world.
The psalmist asks for deliverance for “your beloved,” and makes a twofold request to the LORD: save with your right hand and answer me.
The psalmist recalls God’s word spoken in holiness, and then describes the division and measuring out of Shechem and the Valley of Succoth.
The verse lists various regions and tribes: Gilead, Manasseh, Ephraim, and Judah, while symbolically describing Ephraim as the stronghold of the head and Judah as the lawgiver.
Moab, Edom, and Philistia are mentioned in the context of conflict: Moab is described as a washbasin, a sandal is thrown over Edom, and the psalmist triumphs over Philistia.
The psalmist asks who will lead him to a fortified city and guide him to Edom; the question emphasizes the need for direction and help.
The psalm mentions a situation of rejection and weakness, in which God has not gone out with the armies of the people, and immediately afterward asks for help against the adversary.
The conclusion expresses confidence: with God’s help, victory will be achieved, and he will defeat the adversaries; this emphasizes that deliverance does not depend on human strength alone.
